title: Leonberg to Bad Ragaz: Nature the Visible Spirit
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Leonberg, the deacon's house below the Schloss
stops.campa: In the little Württemberg town of Leonberg, in the house of the deacon Joseph Friedrich Schelling, a son is born on the twenty-seventh of January and named Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph. The father is an orientalist and scholar of scripture; the household breathes Hebrew, Greek and the old theology. The child reads early and devours everything set before him, a prodigy the family cannot keep pace with. Above the roofs stands the ducal Schloss; below runs the ordinary Swabian world into which a most unquiet spirit has entered.

stops.name: Nürtingen, the Latin school
stops.campa: The boy is sent down the Neckar to the Latin school at Nürtingen, where the sons of Swabia are drilled in the ancient tongues. He masters them faster than his masters can teach, outrunning boys twice his age. Here too, in this small town, walks another schoolboy: Friedrich Hölderlin, older, dreaming already of Greece, whose path will braid with his for life. The seed of the coming friendship is planted in the ordinary dust of a provincial classroom.

stops.name: Bebenhausen, the cloister school
stops.campa: His father is appointed to the monastic school lodged in the old Cistercian cloister of Bebenhausen, in the wooded hills above Tübingen, and the family follows. Among the silent Gothic vaults and the fishponds of the monks the boy grows in learning under his father's eye, steeped in the Bible and the classics. So gifted is he that the theological seminary at Tübingen, which by rule admits no one under eighteen, will open its gates to him at fifteen, a dispensation granted to genius.

segments.name: The Tübingen Stift and the German Dawn (1790–1795)

stops.name: Tübingen, the Stift, the shared attic room
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of October, aged fifteen, Schelling enters the Tübinger Stift, the Lutheran seminary in its great house above the Neckar. Into one narrow chamber fate gathers three: Schelling the boy-prodigy, the grave Hegel, and the luminous Hölderlin. They share the attic, the plain fare, the enforced theology they inwardly resist. Under the vaulted roof they read Kant, Plato and Spinoza by candlelight and forge among themselves the covenant of a whole age. The German dawn is kindled in a student's cell.

stops.name: Tübingen, the master's dissertation on the origin of evil
stops.campa: Aged seventeen, Schelling takes his master's degree with a Latin dissertation on the oldest myth of the Fall: the third chapter of Genesis, the serpent, the tree, the origin of human evil. It is the question that will govern his whole life and return transfigured in the Freedom essay of his manhood: whence evil, if all things flow from God? Already in the Stift the boy circles the abyss the grown philosopher will name. The keynote of his thought is struck before he is a man.
suggested_refs: Antiquissimi de prima malorum humanorum origine (1792)

stops.name: Tübingen, the Tree of Liberty in the meadow
stops.campa: News of the Revolution crosses the Rhine and sets the seminarians ablaze. Schelling, who has rendered the Marseillaise into German, goes out with Hegel and Hölderlin into a meadow by the Neckar and there they plant a Tree of Liberty. Around it the three dance and swear eternal fidelity to freedom and to the great struggle for the liberation of mankind. The tale will be doubted by later sober men, but it is told, and it tells the truth of their hearts: three who will remake philosophy first vowed themselves to liberty around a sapling.
suggested_refs: Schelling's German translation of the Marseillaise

stops.name: Tübingen, the first philosophy, the break toward Fichte
stops.campa: Still a student, not yet twenty, Schelling publishes On the Possibility of a Form of Philosophy in General, and Fichte himself takes notice of the boy from the Stift. The next year comes the Philosophical Letters on Dogmatism and Criticism. The theology the seminary would impose falls away; the young man has become a philosopher of the first rank while his elders still call him pupil. He completes his doctoral work on the heretic Marcion and turns his face to the wider world.
stops.quote: There is in the last and highest instance no other being than willing. Willing is primordial being.
stops.quote_source: Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom (1809), the mature formula of the freedom he first tasted at Tübingen
suggested_refs: Vom Ich als Prinzip der Philosophie (1795)
Philosophische Briefe über Dogmatismus und Kritizismus

segments.name: Leipzig and the Turn to Nature (1796–1798)

stops.name: Leipzig, tutor to the young barons, the sciences
stops.campa: Schelling takes a post as tutor to two young barons von Riedesel and comes with them to Leipzig. In the university's lecture halls he throws himself upon the new natural science: chemistry, physics, medicine, the electricity of Galvani, the ferment of living things. Here the great intuition seizes him: nature is no dead mechanism but a living power, spirit in the making. Out of Leipzig will come the Naturphilosophie, the vision that nature is spirit visible and spirit invisible nature.
stops.quote: Nature should be spirit made visible, spirit invisible nature.
stops.quote_source: Ideas for a Philosophy of Nature (Ideen zu einer Philosophie der Natur, 1797), Introduction
suggested_refs: Ideen zu einer Philosophie der Natur (1797)
University of Leipzig lecture halls c.1796

stops.name: Leipzig, On the World-Soul, the one life in all things
stops.campa: From Leipzig Schelling sends out On the World-Soul, reviving the ancient dream of a single animating power that binds the organic and inorganic worlds into one living whole. Magnetism, electricity, chemistry, life: all are graded expressions of one force polarising itself through nature. It is this book, poetic and daring, that will reach Goethe in Weimar and win the young man his chair. The philosophy of nature stands complete in outline before its author is twenty-three.

stops.name: Dresden, the galleries, the meeting of the Romantics
stops.campa: In Dresden Schelling stands before the treasures of the gallery and meets the gathering brotherhood of the new Romanticism: the Schlegel brothers, Novalis, and Caroline, wife of August Wilhelm Schlegel, the most brilliant woman of the age. Amid the Raphaels and the winter light of Saxony, art, philosophy and nature are proclaimed one. He is not yet twenty-three, and already the circle that will make Jena the capital of the German spirit forms around him.

stops.name: Weimar, Goethe calls the young man to Jena
stops.campa: Goethe, minister of Saxe-Weimar, reads On the World-Soul and is captivated by the poetry of this philosophy of nature. It answers his own dream of the living whole, the one metamorphosing power beneath all forms. He summons the youth to a chair at Jena. The blessing of the greatest German is laid upon the Naturphilosophie: the old poet and the young philosopher recognize in each other a single vision of nature as creative spirit, and the appointment is made.
stops.quote: History as a whole is a progressive, gradually self-disclosing revelation of the Absolute.

stops.name: Jena, professor at twenty-three
stops.campa: In October, aged twenty-three, Schelling mounts the rostrum of the University of Jena as extraordinary professor of philosophy. Fichte is his colleague, Hegel will soon follow, and the students crowd to hear the wonder-boy of German thought. Around him blazes the Jena of Novalis, the Schlegels, Tieck and Schleiermacher: the brief incandescent spring in which the moderns declare the self and nature reconciled. He is the youngest star, and for a moment the brightest.

stops.name: Jena, the First Outline of a System of the Philosophy of Nature
stops.campa: Schelling pours out book after book in Jena: the First Outline of a System of the Philosophy of Nature and its Introduction. Nature is no finished product but pure productivity, an infinite becoming forever checked and quickened into forms, the same creative power that in man wakes to consciousness of itself. Around him the Romantic house on the Leutragasse fills with Caroline's wit and the Schlegels' talk; Novalis and Tieck come and go. Jena is the burning centre of the world, and Schelling its philosopher of the living earth.
suggested_refs: Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie (1799)

stops.name: Jena, the System of Transcendental Idealism
stops.campa: In 1800 Schelling gives the age its keystone: the System of Transcendental Idealism, which climbs from the I to nature and back, and crowns philosophy with art, where the conscious and unconscious meet in one flame. The next year, in the Presentation of My System, he proclaims the absolute Identity: nature and spirit two faces of one indifferent ground. Here the friendship with Fichte breaks: nature, Schelling declares, is not a mere posit of the ego but a power in its own right, spirit still asleep.

stops.name: Bamberg, the fateful journey south with Caroline and Auguste
stops.campa: In the spring of 1800 Caroline travels south into Franconia with her daughter Auguste and with Schelling, seeking a cure and, some whisper, cover for a love not yet lawful. They come to Bamberg but find no house, and press on toward the little bath of Bocklet. Schelling, deep in the medical enthusiasms of his Naturphilosophie, takes a hand in the girl's regimen. The journey that should have brought healing carries them instead toward the grief that will bind and haunt them.

stops.name: Bocklet, the death of Auguste, the shadow on the love
stops.campa: At the little Franconian spa of Bocklet, where Caroline has come with her beloved daughter Auguste and with Schelling, the girl of fifteen falls ill of dysentery on the first of July and dies on the twelfth. Schelling, versed in medicine, had counselled her treatment; the malicious tongues of Jena will whisper that his hand hastened her end. It is a lie, but it wounds. The great love of Schelling and Caroline is baptized in grief, and their bond is sealed over an open grave.

stops.name: Jena, Hegel arrives, the Critical Journal of the two friends
stops.campa: Hegel, the grave companion of the attic room, comes at last to Jena, drawn by Schelling's fame, and habilitates under his younger friend's protection. Together in 1802 they found the Critical Journal of Philosophy and wage joint war on the half-thinkers of the day; Hegel's first book defends the difference between Fichte's and Schelling's systems in Schelling's favour. For a season the two who danced round the Tree of Liberty stand shoulder to shoulder again, before the ways divide forever.
suggested_refs: Hegel, Differenz des Fichteschen und Schellingschen Systems (1801)

stops.name: Murrhardt, the marriage to Caroline
stops.campa: Goethe himself smooths the way to Caroline's divorce from Schlegel. On the twenty-sixth of June, in the church of St. Januarius at Murrhardt, Schelling's own father the deacon joins the two who have loved through scandal and death. Caroline, witty, fierce, the soul of the Romantic circle, won from the great Schlegel, becomes his wife. Hölderlin, the third of the attic room, is seen at the wedding, already darkening toward his long night. The great love is consecrated in Swabia.

segments.name: Würzburg and Munich: Identity and Sorrow (1803–1820)

stops.name: Würzburg, the professor's chair in Franconia
stops.campa: Schelling and Caroline move to Würzburg, where he takes a chair at the university and delivers his Lectures on the Method of Academic Study, a whole philosophy of knowledge and of the university as the shrine of the Absolute. The Identity philosophy stands at its height: God, nature, art and history all folds of one indivisible reason. But the ground shifts beneath Catholic Franconia, the political weather turns, and within three years the chair is lost.
suggested_refs: Vorlesungen über die Methode des akademischen Studiums (1803)

stops.name: Munich, the Academy, the quarrel with Hegel begins
stops.campa: Called to Munich, Schelling enters the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and becomes secretary of the Academy of Fine Arts. In this year Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit reaches him, and in its preface he reads himself mocked: the Absolute as the night in which all cows are black. The friendship of the attic room curdles into the great feud of German philosophy. On the Deities of Samothrace and the essays on freedom will grow from these Munich years, but a coldness has entered the world.

stops.name: Munich, the Freedom essay, evil and the ground of being
stops.campa: Schelling publishes the Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom, the last work he sends fully finished into the world. Here he descends into the dark ground of God, the abyss beneath the light, and dares to think evil not as mere lack but as a real power springing from the same root as good. Freedom is the capacity for good and evil; willing is primordial being. In this book the whole later theology of the German nineteenth century is prophesied.
stops.quote: God is Life, and not merely Being.
stops.quote_source: Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom (Freiheitsschrift, 1809)
suggested_refs: Schelling on the ground of being

stops.name: Maulbronn, the death of Caroline
stops.campa: At the old cloister-town of Maulbronn, whither they have travelled, Caroline is taken by dysentery. In the small hours of the seventh of September she dies in Schelling's arms; she is buried two days later in the churchyard. The great love is ended. Schelling is broken as he will never wholly mend; the man of light has met the reality of death and loss he wrote of in the Freedom essay. From this grave springs the meditation on immortality and the long, silent, unfinished labour of The Ages of the World.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Private Lectures on the whole system
stops.campa: In Stuttgart, before a small circle, Schelling delivers the Private Lectures, a last spoken summa of his system from God through nature to spirit and the fall. Still under the shadow of Caroline's death, he wrestles with the descent of the Absolute into the world and the possibility of return. He begins to write The Ages of the World, drafting and redrafting the primordial past of God, and never finishes it, the greatest unpublished ruin of German idealism.

segments.name: The Long Silence: Erlangen and Munich (1812–1841)

stops.name: Munich, second marriage to Pauline Gotter
stops.campa: Caroline's dear friend Pauline Gotter becomes Schelling's second wife, and out of the wreck of grief a quieter household rises; children are born, the years steady. But the great published torrent has stopped. Schelling withdraws into administration, into the Academy, into vast private manuscripts no reader sees. The world begins to speak of him in the past tense, as of a comet burned out, while Hegel's system conquers the German universities. The long silence settles over the philosopher of nature.

stops.name: Munich, On the Deities of Samothrace, the descent into myth
stops.campa: Before the Bavarian Academy Schelling reads On the Deities of Samothrace, plunging into the dark Cabiri, the primal hungering gods of the Samothracian mysteries, seeking in the oldest cults the ladder by which the divine ascends into being. It is a fragment torn from the vast unfinished Ages of the World, over whose first book he labours and despairs, printing and suppressing draft after draft. The philosopher of nature has become the archaeologist of God's own past, digging beneath the light for the ground of all things.
suggested_refs: Die Weltalter (Ages of the World) drafts

stops.name: Erlangen, the lectures in the wilderness
stops.campa: From 1820 Schelling lectures at Erlangen, holding still his Munich post. In these small Franconian halls he turns from the finished systems of his youth toward a new thing: the Philosophy of Mythology, the idea that the gods of the nations are not errors but a true theogonic process working itself out in human consciousness. The seed of the final philosophy of revelation is sown in near-obscurity, spoken to few, while the age looks the other way.

stops.name: Munich, the new university chair, positive philosophy
stops.campa: The Bavarian university is moved to Munich and Schelling takes a chair there, drawing crowds again as the old lion of German thought. He forges the distinction that will crown his life: negative philosophy, which thinks only what a thing must be, against positive philosophy, which thinks the fact that it is: the free act of a living God who reveals himself in history. The dead Hegel's system, he prophesies, cannot cross from thought to existence. Schelling prepares his return.

segments.name: Berlin: Against the Dead Hegel's Shadow (1841–1846)

stops.name: Berlin, summoned to slay the dragon of Hegelianism
stops.campa: The King of Prussia calls the aged Schelling to Berlin, to the very chair where Hegel taught and died, expressly to root out the pantheism and the revolution that have grown from Hegel's school. On the fifteenth of November he mounts the rostrum before an overflowing hall. In the audience sit Kierkegaard, Engels, Bakunin, Burckhardt, Humboldt: the whole coming century, listening. The old man who once planted a Tree of Liberty is set against the shade of his oldest friend, to speak the Philosophy of Revelation.
stops.quote: I am so glad to have heard Schelling's second lecture — indescribable. When he mentioned the word 'actuality' the child of thought leaped for joy within me as in Elizabeth.
stops.quote_source: Søren Kierkegaard, journal / letter, Berlin, November 1841
suggested_refs: Kierkegaard's notes on Schelling's Berlin lectures

stops.name: Berlin, the Philosophy of Revelation, and disillusion
stops.campa: Through the winter Schelling unfolds the Philosophy of Mythology and of Revelation: the descent of the divine into history, Christ as the turning of the ages, myth fulfilled in the incarnate God. But the young Hegelians turn on him. Engels writes his savage pamphlet Schelling and Revelation; Kierkegaard sickens of the 'insufferable nonsense' and departs. When Paulus pirates the lectures verbatim, Schelling, robbed of his words, falls silent and lectures no more. The last great effort ends in wounded quiet.
suggested_refs: Friedrich Engels, Schelling und die Offenbarung (1842)

stops.name: Bad Ragaz, death at the healing waters
stops.campa: In the summer of his eightieth year Schelling comes to the Swiss spa of Bad Ragaz, to the healing springs of the Tamina gorge under the Alps. There, on the twentieth of August, the last of the great German idealists lays down his life: the boy of Leonberg, the youth of the attic room, the professor at twenty-three, the philosopher of nature and freedom and revelation. King Maximilian of Bavaria raises over his grave a stone that names him the first thinker of Germany. Nature, made visible spirit, receives him.
suggested_refs: Tamina gorge and springs, Bad Ragaz
